I ran the lean package of the claimed closure of Navier Stokes by OpenAI. Built the repository, ran comparator. It compiles with three standard axioms.

Repository: https://github.com/elmismisimoxhunca/NavierStokes-OpenAI-Verification

You can independently rerun everything, take in mind it requires a beefy PC.

Ongoing controversy aside, it compiles cleanly and did not fail any tests.

There are statements in https://github.com/lean-dojo/LeanMillenniumPrizeProblems/blob/main/Problems/NavierStokes/Millennium.lean and https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/main/FormalConjectures/Millenium/NavierStokes.lean

It uses the formal conjectures version here: https://github.com/openai/NavierStokesAndEuler/blob/8937a8f4cbc7abaab5e9e97d1cc7f5d2319d9538/NavierStokes/ComparatorDefinitions.lean which is almost a copy of the original NavierStokes.lean file.
Which I wrote mostly :) It got looked over by couple of actual mathematicians but at this point it deserves a bigger scrutiny

And the resolved C and D statements from formal conjectures NavierStokes.lean are here https://github.com/openai/NavierStokesAndEuler/blob/8937a8f4cbc7abaab5e9e97d1cc7f5d2319d9538/NavierStokes/ComparatorSolution.lean
@Bilal What do you mean by verification? Isn't the result verified with comparator already?

@metakuntyyy
For example, Clay states the forcing decay condition in terms of bounds on all mixed partial derivatives $\partial_x^\alpha \partial_t^m f$, while the Lean formalization packages this using iteratedFDerivWithin on space-time. Comparator can verify the Lean theorem, but it doesn’t by itself tell us that this formal encoding is exactly equivalent to Clay’s intended condition. That kind of statement-audit is what I had in mind.

My view is that there are two things missing for verification:

  1. community agreement that the statement is correct. @Moritz Firsching said it seems to be using the statement from @Tomas Skrivan in the Formal Conjectures project, but I don’t know how closely this has been checked. Also Formal Conjectures has had mistakes so additional scrutiny would be good like maybe proving other variations of the theorem or known consequences.
  2. Making sure it doesn’t exploit kernel soundness issues. Running with all known external checkers, especially @Joachim Breitner’s lean-inductive-models (since that addresses one of the largest worries about the soundness of Lean’s type theory), and maybe running with a kernel using @Bas Spitters’s verified GMP (a known worry about implementation correctness). I’m sure this is all overkill, but people on X are questioning if it exploited a Lean soundness bug.

(Both are especially overkill since I’m sure Clay and others won’t rest until the proof is understood, but it is a good exercise for the Lean community.)

Given the recent soundness bugs found in the kernel and the increasing ability of AI to corrupt systems, does it make sense to consider that such an exploit might have been used in the formalization? From my POV such exploits rely on meta code which can easily be spotted, but I have no knowledge in this matter so I wonder if it might go undetected.

With Comparator, which this project uses, metaprogramming hacks are largely not possible. The worry is kernel bugs or theory unsoundness. See above for my thoughts on how to try to guard against this, but at the same time I highly doubt a new bug was discovered and used, but I guess we can’t know for sure given the state of Lean’s kernel and type theory.

Then again for the purposes of the formalization one could just add an instance that is just docs#lineDeriv and it should work just fine? I don't know if that is something Mathlib as a whole should have, I guess not

I want to summary the diff:

  1. Changes imports from FC to Mathlib, changes the namespace of the statement and some documentation slightly. This is unimportant.
  2. Removes some FC infrastructure; these are only used for cataloguing. This is unimportant.
  3. Removes versions A,B of the NS conjecture (which afaik are still open). This is to be expected and unimportant.
  4. Changes notation for divergence from notation to local notation. This is unimportant.
  5. Does not open EuclideanGeometry and redefines notation from R^3 and R^n. This is the "most complicated" change. However I checked that this is an identical reimlmentation of the R^n/R^3 notation used in FC (except being local instead of scoped). So: This is unimportant

In summary, the relevant Lean declarations are identical ("syntactically") and all diff cosmetic.

I (let Claude to) did a few further sanity checks:

  1. Run comparator as well.
  2. Verify the equivalence of formal-conjectures formalization, and current lean-dojo formalization.
  3. Verified lean-dojo's version using OpenAI solution & the proven equivalence. Only that there, Claude was not properly Comparator-paranoic, and and compiled OpenAI's proof outside of Sandbox which could have compromised everything... (but it seems enough for me).
If the question is mathematical, I can answer: the formalized statement is true to the statement of the Clay prize, so getting a Lean proof for this formalized statement is all that is needed.

Indeed while I am not exactly as authoritative as @Sébastien Gouëzel, I don't think there is any reasonable doubt over the correctness of the formalization. Since it's a holiday in Barcelona, I tried my hand with Claude at a more slavishly faithful formalization of the official clay statement along the same structure as the existing one:

import Mathlib


open ContDiff Set MeasureTheory
open scoped LineDeriv NNReal ENNReal

namespace NavierStokes.Alternative

local notation "ℝ^" n:65 => EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)
local notation "ℝ³" => EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)

local notation "𝐞" j:max => EuclideanSpace.single j (1 : ℝ)

variable {n : ℕ}

noncomputable scoped instance instLineDerivCoord {F : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup F]
    [NormedSpace ℝ F] : LineDeriv (Fin n) (ℝ^n → F) (ℝ^n → F) where
  lineDerivOp j g := fun x => lineDeriv ℝ g x (𝐞 j)

theorem lineDerivOp_coord_apply {F : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F]
    (j : Fin n) (g : ℝ^n → F) (x : ℝ^n) :
    ∂_{j} g x = lineDeriv ℝ g x (𝐞 j) :=
  rfl

noncomputable scoped instance instLineDerivSpaceTimeCoord {F : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup F]
    [NormedSpace ℝ F] : LineDeriv (Fin n) (ℝ^n × ℝ → F) (ℝ^n × ℝ → F) where
  lineDerivOp j g := fun z => lineDerivWithin ℝ g (univ ×ˢ Ici 0) z (𝐞 j, 0)

theorem lineDerivOp_spaceTimeCoord_apply {F : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F]
    (j : Fin n) (g : ℝ^n × ℝ → F) (z : ℝ^n × ℝ) :
    ∂_{j} g z = lineDerivWithin ℝ g (univ ×ˢ Ici 0) z (𝐞 j, 0) :=
  rfl

noncomputable scoped instance instLineDerivTime {F : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup F]
    [NormedSpace ℝ F] : LineDeriv Unit (ℝ^n × ℝ → F) (ℝ^n × ℝ → F) where
  lineDerivOp _ g := fun z => lineDerivWithin ℝ g (univ ×ˢ Ici 0) z (0, 1)

local notation "∂ₜ" => LineDeriv.lineDerivOp ()

theorem lineDerivOp_time_apply {F : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F]
    (g : ℝ^n × ℝ → F) (z : ℝ^n × ℝ) :
    ∂ₜ g z = lineDerivWithin ℝ g (univ ×ˢ Ici 0) z (0, 1) :=
  rfl

noncomputable
def div {E : Type*} [LineDeriv (Fin n) (E → ℝ^n) (E → ℝ^n)] (v : E → ℝ^n) (x : E) : ℝ :=
  ∑ i : Fin n, ∂_{i} v x i

def IsOnePeriodic {α : Sort*} (f : ℝ^n → α) : Prop :=
  ∀ x i, f (x + 𝐞 i) = f x

structure InitialVelocityCondition (u₀ : ℝ^n → ℝ^n) : Prop where
  div_free : ∀ x, div u₀ x = 0
  smooth : ContDiff ℝ ∞ u₀

structure InitialVelocityConditionDecay (u₀ : ℝ^n → ℝ^n) : Prop extends
    InitialVelocityCondition u₀ where
  decay : ∀ (k : ℕ) (α : Fin k → Fin n) (K : ℝ), ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ x,
    ‖∂^{α} u₀ x‖ ≤ C * (1 + ‖x‖) ^ (-K)

structure InitialVelocityConditionPeriodic (u₀ : ℝ^n → ℝ^n) : Prop extends
    InitialVelocityCondition u₀ where
  isOnePeriodic : IsOnePeriodic u₀

structure ForceCondition (f : ℝ^n × ℝ → ℝ^n) : Prop where
  smooth : ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ f (univ ×ˢ Ici 0)

structure ForceConditionDecay (f : ℝ^n × ℝ → ℝ^n) : Prop extends ForceCondition f where
  decay : ∀ (k : ℕ) (α : Fin k → Fin n) (m : ℕ) (K : ℝ), ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ x, ∀ t ≥ 0,
    ‖∂^{α} (∂ₜ^[m] f) (x, t)‖ ≤ C * (1 + ‖x‖ + t) ^ (-K)

structure ForceConditionPeriodic (f : ℝ^n × ℝ → ℝ^n) : Prop extends ForceCondition f where
  isOnePeriodic : ∀ x t j, t ≥ 0 → f (x + 𝐞 j, t) = f (x, t)
  decay : ∀ (k : ℕ) (α : Fin k → Fin n) (m : ℕ) (K : ℝ), ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ x, ∀ t ≥ 0,
    ‖∂^{α} (∂ₜ^[m] f) (x, t)‖ ≤ C * (1 + |t|) ^ (-K)

structure NavierStokesExistenceAndSmoothness
    (ν : ℝ) (u₀ : ℝ^n → ℝ^n) (f : ℝ^n × ℝ → ℝ^n)
    (u : ℝ^n × ℝ → ℝ^n) (p : ℝ^n × ℝ → ℝ) : Prop where
  navier_stokes : ∀ i x, ∀ t ≥ 0,
    ∂ₜ u (x, t) i + ∑ j, u (x, t) j * ∂_{j} u (x, t) i =
      ν * ∑ j : Fin n, ∂_{j} (∂_{j} u) (x, t) i - ∂_{i} p (x, t) + f (x, t) i
  div_free : ∀ x, ∀ t ≥ 0, div u (x, t) = 0
  initial_condition : ∀ x, u (x, 0) = u₀ x
  velocity_smooth : ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ u (univ ×ˢ Ici 0)
  pressure_smooth : ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ p (univ ×ˢ Ici 0)

structure NavierStokesExistenceAndSmoothnessRn
    (ν : ℝ) (u₀ : ℝ^n → ℝ^n) (f : ℝ^n × ℝ → ℝ^n)
    (u : ℝ^n × ℝ → ℝ^n) (p : ℝ^n × ℝ → ℝ) : Prop
  extends NavierStokesExistenceAndSmoothness ν u₀ f u p where
  globally_bounded_energy : ∃ C : ℝ≥0, ∀ t ≥ 0, ∫⁻ x, ‖u (x, t)‖ₑ ^ 2 < C

structure NavierStokesExistenceAndSmoothnessPeriodic
    (ν : ℝ) (u₀ : ℝ^n → ℝ^n) (f : ℝ^n × ℝ → ℝ^n)
    (u : ℝ^n × ℝ → ℝ^n) (p : ℝ^n × ℝ → ℝ) : Prop
  extends NavierStokesExistenceAndSmoothness ν u₀ f u p where
  isOnePeriodic_velocity : ∀ x t j, t ≥ 0 → u (x + 𝐞 j, t) = u (x, t)
  isOnePeriodic_pressure : ∀ x t j, t ≥ 0 → p (x + 𝐞 j, t) = p (x, t)

theorem navier_stokes_breakdown_R3 (ν : ℝ) (hν : 0 < ν) :
    ∃ (u₀ : ℝ³ → ℝ³) (f : ℝ³ × ℝ → ℝ³),
      InitialVelocityConditionDecay u₀ ∧ ForceConditionDecay f ∧
      ¬ ∃ u p, NavierStokesExistenceAndSmoothnessRn ν u₀ f u p := by
  sorry

theorem navier_stokes_breakdown_periodic (ν : ℝ) (hν : 0 < ν) :
    ∃ (u₀ : ℝ³ → ℝ³) (f : ℝ³ × ℝ → ℝ³),
      InitialVelocityConditionPeriodic u₀ ∧ ForceConditionPeriodic f ∧
      ¬ ∃ u p, NavierStokesExistenceAndSmoothnessPeriodic ν u₀ f u p := by
  sorry

end NavierStokes.Alternative

Claude had no problem proving the equivalence with the FormalConjectures version (which I think is better lean by the way)

I wanted to ask: Did anyone check the Navier-Stokes proof with a verified big-integer library? To me, it feels like exploiting a bug in big-integer libraries is the easiest to camouflage in complex calculations, and also the easiest to exploit multiple big-int libraries at once by writing an expression that gets miscalculated by each, and getting a contradiction by decide.

I think @Joachim Breitner ran con-rust on it which is a verified rust checker with a verified bignum library (but I’m not 100% sure, as I only remember con-leche being mentioned for NS). I can’t remember if @Bas Spitters ran any of his verified bignum kernels on NS. (By the way, this is the extreme downside of the multiple kernel approach to lean trust. No one knows what subset of kernels was used to check a result.)
